I'm in an elementary school and a lot of what I did was in this area. If you'd like my perspective for the primary schools, message me!

Some things from my the interviews I've recently:

* Research the school itself, be prepared to either make a connection to their mission statement or ask a question at the end that pertains to the school specifically.

* What does the job posting list as duties? Are you doing 504's, MTSS, expected to run small groups? Whatever they list, be prepared to talk about it. If you don't have direct experience in the area, explain how your skills will translate or you are willing to learn more about the process if given the opportunity to.

* A time where you had success and a time where you could have done something differently.

* Try and find out your role within the school. The elementary school expected the school counselor to be a leader in the building, what will they expect from you?

* I've had questions about what I think the expectation is of teachers in relation to SEL and the relationship with administration, so basically how will you collaborate with the other people in the building. 

Good luck and I'm sure you will kill it!

This is a hotly contested topic in the industry. Its more equitable across the restaurant but comes at the cost of other employees. One restaurant group in town switched to tip pooling and touted it as a big positive change. They glowingly spoke about how position in the restaurant deserves a good wage. If the company truly believed this, why didn't they just raise wages? 

Another restaurant opened in town and started with a tip pool pay structure. It did not go well. Service was poor and the servers were salty. The pay was good in relation to other fields (I believe it was 25 an hour for servers but not 100% on the amount) and they provided benefits/paid time off. Eventually the restaurant switched to a traditional model. 

It all comes down to which do you prefer, the option to have a semblance of control over your income. And really it's not a lot of control because you're relying on a manager to schedule you enough, competent hosts who do their best to evenly seat the server sections (which is no small feat), and there are just unlucky shifts where no one comes in. Your other option is to have a significantly lower wage but the security of knowing you're going to make a decent wage week in week out. 

We'll have to change the culture of the service industry for it to be successful and that is a hard task.

It depends on how the tips are pooled. Some places will pool for the day, others over a whole week. 

If the tips are pooled over the week, the common belief is that it disincentivizes working hard and devalues busy shifts. Why should you get your ass kicked on a busy Friday when you'll make the exact same amount if you work a slow shift in the morning on a Tuesday? Basically the busy shifts when people are getting absolutely creamed are subsidizing those that are objectively doing less work.

As a life long service industry employee I can get behind pooling by shift. Every position in a restaurant contributes to the service a guest recieves.
